node.label: Margaret C. Jacob
node.date_label: The Radical Enlightenment (1981) · Living the Enlightenment (1991) · Telling the Truth about History, coauthor (1994) · The First Knowledge Economy (2014)
node.description: In The Radical Enlightenment (1981), Jacob located early Enlightenment radicalism in the political and religious conflicts connecting England, the Dutch Republic and French Protestant exiles. Living the Enlightenment (1991) argued that Masonic lodges helped form modern civil society by practising constitutional self-government. Her histories of science connect scientific culture to industry; The First Knowledge Economy (2014) centres mechanical knowledge and its transmission. Erik Hornung praised its evidence about British engineers but questioned whether its Continental comparison used comparable evidence. Jacob’s 2014 retrospective credits Christopher Hill and J. G. A. Pocock while opposing Jonathan Israel’s Spinoza-centred account. Her 2013 Logos essay criticizes Bruno Latour’s approach to historical motives. With Joyce Appleby and Lynn Hunt she coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994), a defence of accountable historical inquiry.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Newtonians and the English Revolution, 1689–1720 (1976); The Radical Enlightenment (1981); The Cultural Meaning of the Scientific Revolution (1988); Living the Enlightenment (1991); Telling the Truth about History (1994), with Joyce Appleby and Lynn Hunt; Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West (1997); The Book That Changed Europe (2010), with Lynn Hunt and Wijnand Mijnhardt; The First Knowledge Economy (2014).
node.scope_note: Read the 2014 Diametros argument and 2013 Logos essay, selected pages of the 2014 introduction, publisher descriptions and author bibliography, and Hornung’s review. The selected monographs were not read in full; Living the Enlightenment, Scientific Culture and Telling the Truth are summarized only at publisher-description level. Hill’s particular work and the date of the Pocock conversations are unidentified.

proposed_edges.relationship: Jacob and Joyce Appleby coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994), with Lynn Hunt.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Substantive monograph coauthorship; author metadata only. The separate 1994 record establishes original year; Norton displays the 1995 paperback.

proposed_edges.relationship: Jacob and Lynn Hunt coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994), with Joyce Appleby.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Substantive monograph coauthorship; author metadata only. Same three-author book as mcj_n_01; no claim about division of chapters.

proposed_edges.relationship: Recalling The Radical Enlightenment (1981) in her 2014 retrospective, Jacob credits Hill’s account of religious and political radicalism within the English Revolution.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Explicit intellectual debt in Jacob’s own retrospective. No particular Hill book is identified; the 1981 original is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2014 retrospective on The Radical Enlightenment (1981), Jacob recalls developing its dialectical approach through conversations with Pocock.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Explicit recollection of conceptual formation; no publication by Pocock or date of conversation is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “How Radical was the Enlightenment?” (2014), Jacob criticizes Israel’s Radical Enlightenment (2001) for centring Spinoza and effacing political context.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Direct, named criticism. Jacob also acknowledges the need to revise her own earlier account; neither original monograph is newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The First Knowledge Economy (2014), Jacob adopts Mokyr’s focus on a small community exchanging technical knowledge, citing The Gifts of Athena (2002).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Body engagement, followed by explicit adoption; note 14 identifies Mokyr’s book and p. 66. Mokyr’s original book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Left, Right and Science” (2013), Jacob criticizes Latour’s approach for failing to explain historically specific religious motives in seventeenth-century science.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary criticism distinguishes religious commitments from money and power. The 1998 chapter and Latour’s originals remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West (1997) connects scientific knowledge with European culture, entrepreneurs and engineers.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description only; it identifies a substantive approach to the history of science. No whole-book reading claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Appleby and Hunt, Jacob’s Telling the Truth about History (1994) defends accountable historical inquiry while accepting some criticism of historical authority.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Joint argument as described by the publisher. Existing roster membership retained; chapters and specific philosophical debts unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Left, Right and Science” (2013), Jacob advocates contextual explanations of anti-science positions that distinguish religious commitments from profit motives.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: An explicit intervention in the science wars, distinct from the specific Latour criticism. Existing roster membership retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: The First Knowledge Economy (2014) explains industrial development through mechanical knowledge and the institutions that circulated it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction read; claim records Jacob’s explanation rather than treating it as a settled causal finding.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his ‘Author’s response’ (2016) to ‘The Enlightenment as Modernity: Jonathan Israel’s Interpretation Across Two Decades’, Jonathan Israel criticised Margaret C. Jacob’s emphasis on Toland’s republican originality, arguing that Toland adopted Spinoza’s philosophical system.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Israel’s response on the review journal’s own page. This is Israel’s explicit criticism of Jacob, not an inference from their differing subjects or a review of Jacob’s book. The passage does not identify a particular Jacob title, so none is assigned to the criticism. The year refers to the response itself.

proposed_edges.relationship: Jacob’s The Radical Enlightenment: Pantheists, Freemasons, and Republicans (1981) helped shape Enlightenment historiography through its category of radical Enlightenment, which Diego Lucci describes as highly influential and subsequently reformulated by Jonathan Israel.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Lucci’s review, especially its substantive discussion of the category and note 7 identifying Jacob’s 1981 book. The endpoint is the existing intellectual-history field; no new Enlightenment endpoint is created. This records reception of a category, without claiming Jacob was its first user in all languages. The reviewed collection and Jacob’s book remain unread.
